items.topic: Immobility — active/passive ROM to prevent contractures
items.stem: An immobilized client is at risk for joint contractures. Which nursing intervention best helps prevent contractures?

options.text: Perform or assist with regular active or passive range-of-motion exercises and encourage early mobility as tolerated
Keep all joints locked in full flexion continuously to "rest" the muscles
Avoid all joint movement until the client is fully ambulatory without assistance
Place the client in one position for the entire shift to reduce turning-related fatigue

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: immobility contributes to joint contractures; mitigate with range-of-motion exercises, weight-bearing, and proper positioning. OpenStax Med-Surg: prolonged immobilization causes contractures; promote early mobility and assess ROM. Merck PT: passive ROM when clients cannot move joints themselves; active ROM when able.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prolonged fixed positioning promotes contractures rather than preventing them.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Waiting until full independent ambulation delays needed ROM and mobility interventions.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prolonged single positioning increases musculoskeletal and skin complications.

items.topic: NGN matrix — immobility ROM/contracture prevention indicated vs not
items.stem: For a bedbound client at risk for contractures from immobility, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Perform scheduled passive ROM for joints the client cannot move independently
Encourage active ROM for joints the client can safely move
Promote early mobility/ambulation as condition allows
Keep extremities rigidly flexed in one position all day to "protect" joints
Omit all ROM because bed rest alone prevents musculoskeletal decline

rationales.R1: Indicated. Passive ROM maintains joint motion when the client cannot participate.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Active ROM is preferred when the client can move safely.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Early mobility helps prevent atrophy and contractures.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Prolonged fixed positioning causes contractures.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Bed rest without ROM increases musculoskeletal complications.

items.topic: PCA — only the patient presses the demand button; lockout prevents overdose
items.stem: A postoperative client has IV patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). Which teaching is most important for safe use?

options.text: Only the client should press the PCA button; family/staff must not press it for the client, and the lockout interval limits extra doses
Family members should press the button whenever the client looks uncomfortable, even if sedated
The nurse should press the button every 5 minutes around the clock regardless of sedation
Anyone may press the button freely because PCA pumps have no dose or time limits

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: no one but the patient should press the button; lockout and alertness are safety measures against overmedication/respiratory depression. Merck: only the patient may push the administration button; lockout dosage/interval prevent extra boluses.
rationales.B: Incorrect. PCA-by-proxy (others pressing) can cause oversedation and respiratory depression.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Staff should not press the demand button for the client as routine "proxy" dosing.
rationales.D: Incorrect. PCA pumps are programmed with lockout and maximum limits.

items.topic: PCA opioids — monitor sedation and respiratory depression
items.stem: A client receiving opioid PCA becomes increasingly difficult to arouse with a decreasing respiratory rate. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Stop/hold further opioid dosing per protocol, support airway/breathing with oxygen as needed, stimulate the client, and notify the provider/rapid response as indicated
Increase the PCA basal rate so pain will not wake the client
Ask family to keep pressing the PCA button until the client is fully asleep
Ignore sedation because PCA lockout makes respiratory depression impossible

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: PCA overmedication can cause sedation and respiratory depression; monitor and intervene. Merck: opioids cause respiratory depression/sedation risk; PCA lockout helps but does not eliminate need for monitoring and response to oversedation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing opioid infusion worsens respiratory depression.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Proxy dosing during sedation is dangerous.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lockout reduces but does not eliminate opioid adverse-effect risk; monitoring is required.

items.jurisdiction_note: Canada — PHAC/Canada.ca tick removal guidance aligned with CDC technique
items.topic: Tick removal — fine tweezers, steady pull; no petroleum jelly
items.stem: A community client finds an attached tick after hiking. Which teaching is correct for immediate removal?

options.text: Use clean fine-tipped tweezers to grasp close to the skin and pull upward with steady, even pressure; then clean the area—do not use petroleum jelly or heat to force detachment
Cover the tick with petroleum jelly or nail polish and wait for it to back out on its own
Burn the tick with a hot match while it is still attached
Twist and jerk the tick body forcefully to remove it quickly

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: fine-tipped tweezers close to skin; steady even pressure; clean site; avoid petroleum jelly/heat/nail polish. Canada.ca/PHAC: fine-point tweezers, slow straight pull; do not burn or smother with petroleum jelly/nail polish.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Smothering methods can agitate the tick and increase infection risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Burning is unsafe and not recommended.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Twisting/jerking can leave mouthparts in the skin.

items.topic: Panic attack — stay with client; calm presence; reduce stimuli; coach slow breathing
items.stem: A client begins an acute panic attack with intense fear and hyperventilation. Which nursing action is best initially?

options.text: Stay with the client, reduce environmental stimuli, speak in short calm statements, and coach slow deep breathing
Leave the client alone in a crowded hallway so they can "tough it out"
Argue that nothing is wrong and demand they immediately stop all symptoms
Start a long detailed lecture on cognitive theory while the client cannot process information

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Psych (Peplau): for panic, stay with the client, keep within eyesight, move to a safe quieter space. OpenStax 17.2: remain calm; coach slow deep breathing; quiet environment; reassure the attack will pass. Cleveland Clinic: stay with them, remain calm, short sentences, deep breathing, reassure temporary safety.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Leaving a panicking client alone increases safety risk and distress.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Arguing increases stimulation and does not help panic-level anxiety.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Complex teaching is ineffective at panic level when processing is impaired.

items.topic: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis — clear liquid diet; avoid high fiber during inflammation
items.stem: A client with uncomplicated diverticulitis is being managed with bowel rest at home. Which dietary teaching is most appropriate during the acute inflammatory phase?

options.text: Use a clear liquid diet for a short period as directed, then advance as pain improves; high-fiber foods are avoided while the bowel is inflamed
Immediately start a very high-fiber diet with raw vegetables, nuts, and seeds during peak inflammation
Eat only fried fatty meats and stop all fluids
Force large high-fiber meals every hour to "scrub" the diverticula

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: clear liquid diet for 2–3 days in uncomplicated diverticulitis with advancement when pain abates. OpenStax Med-Surg: liquid diet to rest intestines. OpenStax Nutrition: high fiber contraindicated during diverticulitis inflammation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. High fiber is contraindicated during acute GI inflammation/diverticulitis.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Fluids/clear liquids support bowel rest; fried meats are not the acute plan.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Aggressive high-fiber feeding during acute inflammation is contraindicated.

items.jurisdiction_note: Ontario — CNO Professional Misconduct + Code of Conduct reporting accountabilities
items.topic: CNO — report unsafe practice/unethical conduct to employer or appropriate authority
items.stem: An Ontario nurse observes a colleague's unsafe practice that places clients at risk. Aside from mandatory sexual-abuse reporting rules, what is the nurse's professional accountability?

options.text: Report the unsafe practice or unethical conduct to the appropriate authority (typically the employer/supervisor, and CNO when indicated) because client safety comes first
Stay silent forever because only sexual abuse can ever be reported
Post the colleague's name and client details on social media for public shaming
Ignore client risk to avoid uncomfortable workplace conversations

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Professional Misconduct: failing to report unsafe practice/unethical conduct to the employer/other authority or CNO is misconduct; generally report to employer. OpenStax Med-Surg: nurses must act on incompetent/unethical practice—address colleague/manager and escalate to licensing boards if uncorrected. Client safety is primary.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Sexual-abuse reporting is mandatory to CNO, but nurses also must address/report other unsafe/unethical conduct.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Public posting of PHI and unprofessional shaming violates privacy and professional standards.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Client safety is the primary responsibility.
